title: UP BOARD CLASS 11 — English | Verbs Tenses Present Past Future
description: Subject-wise test on Verbs Tenses Present Past Future (English) for UP BOARD CLASS 11. 50Q.
subject: upbo11-english
instructions: Topic: Verbs Tenses Present Past Future

questions.question: Choose the correct form of the verb to complete the sentence: The Earth ____ around the Sun.

options.explanation: Incorrect tense for a universal truth.
Incorrect tense for a singular subject.
Correct form of the verb for a singular subject in Simple Present tense.
Incorrect tense for a universal truth.

questions.explanation: This describes a universal truth, which always uses the Simple Present tense. For a singular subject like 'The Earth', the verb takes an '-s' ending.
questions.hint: Universal truths use the Simple Present tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate tense: I ____ a new bicycle yesterday.

options.explanation: Incorrect tense for past action.
Incorrect tense for past action.
Incorrect tense for past action.
Correct Simple Past tense form of 'buy'.

questions.explanation: The adverb 'yesterday' clearly indicates a completed action in the past, hence requiring the Simple Past tense of the verb 'buy', which is 'bought'.
questions.hint: The word 'yesterday' indicates past tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Identify the sentence that correctly uses the Future Simple tense.

options.text: She goes to the market tomorrow.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense for future action.

options.text: She will go to the market tomorrow.
options.explanation: Correct Future Simple tense usage.

options.text: She went to the market tomorrow.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense for future action.

options.text: She is going to the market yesterday.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense and adverb usage.

questions.explanation: The Future Simple tense is formed with 'will' + base form of the verb, used for actions that will happen in the future, indicated by 'tomorrow'.
questions.hint: Future Simple tense uses 'will' + base verb.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is in the Present Continuous tense?

options.explanation: Simple Present tense.
Simple Past tense.
Correct Present Continuous tense usage.
Future Simple tense.

questions.explanation: The Present Continuous tense describes an action happening at the moment of speaking or around the present time, formed with 'is/am/are' + verb-ing.
questions.hint: Present Continuous tense uses 'is/am/are' + verb-ing.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Complete the sentence with the most suitable tense: I ____ this movie before, so I don't want to watch it again.

options.explanation: Simple Past tense does not show present relevance.
Correct Present Perfect tense usage.
Past Perfect tense is incorrect here.
Present Continuous tense is incorrect.

questions.explanation: The action of seeing the movie happened at an unspecified time in the past but has a direct relevance to the present ('don't want to watch it again'). This calls for the Present Perfect tense.
questions.hint: Present Perfect tense is used for past actions with present relevance.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct sequence of tenses for the sentence: While she ____ (cook) dinner, the phone ____ (ring).

options.explanation: Both actions in Simple Past tense are incorrect.
Correct sequence: Past Continuous for ongoing action, Simple Past for interruption.
Incorrect tense sequence.
Both actions in Past Continuous tense are incorrect.

questions.explanation: The action of 'cooking' was an ongoing activity in the past (Past Continuous), which was interrupted by a sudden, completed action of the 'phone ringing' (Simple Past).
questions.hint: Past Continuous for ongoing action, Simple Past for interrupted action.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct tense: By the time you arrive, I ____ (finish) my homework.

options.explanation: Simple Present tense is incorrect.
Simple Future tense is incorrect.
Correct Future Perfect tense usage.
Present Continuous tense is incorrect.

questions.explanation: 'By the time you arrive' indicates a point in the future by which another action will be completed. This structure requires the Future Perfect tense ('will have' + past participle).
questions.hint: Future Perfect tense is used for actions completed before a future time.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct conditional sentence (Type 1).

options.text: If it will rain, we will postpone the match.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense in 'if' clause.

options.text: If it rains, we will postpone the match.
options.explanation: Correct Type 1 conditional sentence.

options.text: If it rained, we will postpone the match.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense in 'if' clause.

options.text: If it is raining, we will postpone the match.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense in 'if' clause.

questions.explanation: In a Type 1 conditional sentence (referring to a possible future condition and its probable result), the 'if' clause uses the Simple Present tense, and the main clause uses the Future Simple tense.
questions.hint: Type 1 conditional uses Simple Present in 'if' clause and Future Simple in main clause.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct tense to complete the sentence: He was exhausted because he ____ (run) for an hour without a break.

options.explanation: Simple Past tense is incorrect.
Past Perfect tense is incorrect.
Correct Past Perfect Continuous tense usage.
Present Perfect Continuous tense is incorrect.

questions.explanation: His exhaustion (Past Simple) was a result of an action that had been continuously ongoing for a duration *before* that past point. This requires the Past Perfect Continuous tense to show the duration of the preceding action.
questions.hint: Past Perfect Continuous tense is used for actions that were ongoing before a past point.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Identify the sentence with an incorrect tense usage.

options.text: When I opened the door, it was raining heavily.
options.explanation: Correct tense usage.

options.text: She told me that she had completed her project the previous day.
options.explanation: Correct tense usage.

options.text: If I were a bird, I would fly.
options.explanation: Correct tense usage for hypothetical condition.

options.text: He has been waiting for the bus for two hours when I saw him.
options.explanation: Incorrect tense usage; should be 'had been waiting'.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'when I saw him' (Simple Past) indicates a specific point in the past. To describe an action that was ongoing for a duration *up to* that point in the past, the Past Perfect Continuous tense ('had been waiting') should be used, not the Present Perfect Continuous ('has been waiting').
questions.hint: Past Perfect Continuous tense is required for actions ongoing up to a past point.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence that uses the simple present tense appropriately.

options.text: The earth revolve around the sun.
options.explanation: The verb 'revolve' does not agree with the third person singular subject 'The earth'.

options.text: The earth is revolving around the sun.
options.explanation: The present continuous tense is not used for universal truths.

options.text: The earth revolves around the sun.
options.explanation: The verb 'revolves' agrees with the third person singular subject 'The earth'.

options.text: The earth revolved around the sun.
options.explanation: The simple past tense is not used for universal truths.

questions.explanation: For universal truths and scientific facts, the simple present tense is used. The third person singular subject 'The earth' requires the verb to end in '-s'.
questions.hint: Universal truths and scientific facts use the simple present tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: My brother ______ (visit) his grandparents last weekend.

options.explanation: The simple present tense is not used for past actions.
The present perfect tense is not used for past actions with a specific time reference.
The simple past tense 'visited' correctly fits the context.
The future tense is not used for past actions.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'last weekend' indicates a completed action in the past, thus requiring the simple past tense form of the verb 'visit,' which is 'visited.'
questions.hint: The phrase 'last weekend' indicates a past action.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Which sentence correctly expresses a future action?

options.text: She is going to Delhi next month.
options.explanation: The present continuous tense with 'going to' correctly expresses a future plan.

options.text: She went to Delhi next month.
options.explanation: The simple past tense is not used for future actions.

options.text: She has gone to Delhi next month.
options.explanation: The present perfect tense is not used for future actions.

options.text: She goes to Delhi next month.
options.explanation: The simple present tense is not used for future actions.

questions.explanation: The present continuous tense with a future time expression ('next month') is often used to express definite future plans or arrangements. 'Going to' is also a common way to express future plans.
questions.hint: Future plans can be expressed using the present continuous tense or 'going to'.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Identify the sentence that uses the Present Continuous Tense correctly for an action happening at the moment of speaking.

options.text: Birds usually sing in the morning.
options.explanation: The simple present tense is used for habitual actions, not actions happening at the moment.

options.text: The children are playing in the park right now.
options.explanation: The present continuous tense correctly describes an action happening at the moment.

options.text: My father reads the newspaper every day.
options.explanation: The simple present tense is used for habitual actions, not actions happening at the moment.

options.text: We watched a movie last night.
options.explanation: The simple past tense is not used for actions happening at the moment.

questions.explanation: The present continuous tense (is/am/are + verb-ing) is primarily used for actions happening at the moment of speaking, often indicated by words like 'right now.'
questions.hint: Look for the phrase 'right now' to identify the correct tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Select the most appropriate tense for the blank: I ______ (live) in this city since 2010.

options.explanation: The simple past tense does not indicate a duration up to the present.
The present perfect tense 'have lived' correctly indicates a duration from 2010 to the present.
The present continuous tense is not used for actions with a duration up to the present.
The past perfect tense is not used for actions continuing up to the present.

questions.explanation: The word 'since' indicates a period of time from a specific past point up to the present, requiring the present perfect tense (have/has + past participle).
questions.hint: The word 'since' indicates a duration starting from the past up to the present.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Convert the following sentence into Indirect Speech: 'She said, 'I had already eaten lunch.''

options.text: She said that she has already eaten lunch.
options.explanation: The tense changes incorrectly from Past Perfect to Present Perfect.

options.text: She said that she had already eaten lunch.
options.explanation: The Past Perfect Tense remains unchanged in indirect speech.

options.text: She said that she would already eat lunch.
options.explanation: The tense changes incorrectly to future in the past.

options.text: She said that she already ate lunch.
options.explanation: The tense changes incorrectly to simple past.

questions.explanation: When the direct speech is in the Past Perfect Tense, it generally does not change in Indirect Speech if the reporting verb is in the past tense.
questions.hint: The Past Perfect Tense in direct speech often remains unchanged in indirect speech.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Complete the sentence with the correct tense: If you study hard, you ______ (pass) the exam.

options.explanation: The simple present tense is not used in the main clause of a Type 1 conditional.
The simple future tense 'will pass' correctly completes the Type 1 conditional sentence.
The conditional 'would pass' is used for Type 2 or 3 conditionals, not Type 1.
The past perfect tense is not used in Type 1 conditionals.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 1 conditional sentence (real or likely condition). The 'if' clause uses the simple present tense, and the main clause uses the simple future tense.
questions.hint: Type 1 conditionals use the simple present tense in the 'if' clause and the simple future tense in the main clause.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that has an error in tense usage: He is waiting for his results for two weeks now.

options.explanation: The present continuous tense 'is waiting' does not correctly indicate a duration from the past to the present.
This phrase is grammatically correct.
This phrase correctly indicates a duration.
There is an error in the sentence.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'for two weeks now' indicates an action that started in the past and is continuing up to the present, which requires the present perfect continuous tense ('He has been waiting').
questions.hint: The phrase 'for two weeks now' indicates a duration from the past to the present.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly describes an action that was ongoing before another past action.

options.text: When I entered the room, he was sleeping for three hours.
options.explanation: The past continuous tense does not emphasize the duration before another past action.

options.text: When I entered the room, he had slept for three hours.
options.explanation: The past perfect tense does not emphasize the ongoing nature of the action.

options.text: When I entered the room, he had been sleeping for three hours.
options.explanation: The past perfect continuous tense correctly describes an action ongoing before another past action.

options.text: When I entered the room, he slept for three hours.
options.explanation: The simple past tense does not emphasize the ongoing nature of the action.

questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous tense (had been + verb-ing) is used to show an action that started in the past, continued for some duration, and was still ongoing or had just stopped at another specific point in the past ('When I entered the room'). This emphasizes the duration of the activity before the second past event.
questions.hint: Look for the past perfect continuous tense to describe an action ongoing before another past action.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

Reason (R): This sentence is an example of the Third Conditional, used to express a hypothetical situation in the past and its imagined consequence, following the structure 'If + Past Perfect, Subject + would have + Past Participle'.

options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are correct, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.explanation: The reason is a correct explanation of the assertion.

options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.

questions.hint: The Third Conditional is used for hypothetical situations in the past.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: Look! The children ______ in the park right now.

options.explanation: The Simple Present tense is used for habitual actions, not actions happening at the moment.
The Simple Past tense is used for completed actions in the past, not for actions happening now.
The Present Continuous tense correctly describes an action happening at the moment of speaking.
The Present Perfect tense is used for actions completed at an unspecified time, not for actions happening now.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'right now' indicates an action happening at the moment of speaking, which requires the Present Continuous tense (subject + is/am/are + verb-ing).
questions.hint: The action is happening at the current moment.

questions.question: Identify the sentence that uses the Simple Past Tense correctly:

options.text: She has gone to the market yesterday.
options.explanation: The Present Perfect tense cannot be used with a specific past time marker like 'yesterday'.

options.explanation: The Simple Present tense is incorrect for a completed past action.

options.explanation: The Past Continuous tense describes an ongoing action in the past, not a completed one.

questions.hint: The action was completed in the past.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: Every morning, the sun ______ in the east.

options.explanation: The base form of the verb is incorrect for a singular subject in the Simple Present tense.
The Simple Past tense is incorrect for a habitual action.
The Simple Present tense with '-s' ending correctly describes a habitual action.
The Present Continuous tense is incorrect for a habitual action.

questions.explanation: This sentence describes a universal truth or a habitual action, which requires the Simple Present tense. For a singular subject ('the sun'), the verb takes an '-s' or '-es' ending.

questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct option to express a future plan or intention: We ______ visit our grandparents next weekend.

options.explanation: The Simple Past tense is incorrect for a future action.
The Simple Present tense is incorrect for a future plan.
The Present Perfect tense is incorrect for a future action.
The Simple Future tense correctly expresses a future plan.

questions.question: Select the sentence where the Present Perfect Tense is used appropriately:

options.text: I have seen him last week.
options.explanation: The Present Perfect tense cannot be used with a specific past time marker like 'last week'.

options.text: They have completed their homework tomorrow.
options.explanation: The Present Perfect tense cannot be used with a future time marker like 'tomorrow'.

options.text: She has lived in Delhi for five years.
options.explanation: The Present Perfect tense correctly describes an action that began in the past and continues to the present.

options.text: We have gone to the party an hour ago.
options.explanation: The Present Perfect tense cannot be used with a specific past time marker like 'an hour ago'.

questions.explanation: The Present Perfect tense is used for actions that began in the past and continue into the present, or for past actions with a result in the present. 'For five years' indicates a duration up to the present, making option C correct. Options A and D incorrectly use past time markers with the Present Perfect. Option B incorrectly uses a future time marker.
questions.hint: The action started in the past and continues to the present.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Complete the sentence with the correct past tense form: When I arrived at the station, the train ______ already ______.

options.explanation: The Past Continuous tense describes an ongoing action in the past, not an action completed before another past action.
The Present Perfect tense is incorrect for a past action completed before another past action.
The Past Perfect tense correctly describes an action completed before another past action.
The modal 'would' is incorrect for describing a completed past action.

questions.explanation: This sentence describes two past actions. The train leaving happened before the speaker arrived. To indicate an action completed before another past action, the Past Perfect tense (had + past participle) is used for the earlier action.
questions.hint: The train left before the speaker arrived.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Identify the correct usage of tenses in a conditional sentence (Type 1):

options.text: If it rains, we would stay at home.

options.explanation: The 'if' clause incorrectly uses the Simple Past tense for a Type 1 conditional.

questions.explanation: A Type 1 conditional sentence expresses a real or very likely situation in the future. The 'if' clause uses the Simple Present tense, and the main clause uses the Simple Future tense (will + base verb).

questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the option that correctly uses the Future Continuous tense:

options.text: By this time tomorrow, I will finish my project.

questions.explanation: The Future Continuous tense (will be + verb-ing) is used to describe an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future. 'This time tomorrow' indicates that specific point.

questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Read the following sentence: 'He said, 'I have been waiting for you since morning.'' Which of the following correctly converts the sentence into Indirect Speech, maintaining the correct tense shift?

options.text: He said that he was waiting for me since morning.
options.explanation: The tense shift is incorrect; it should be Past Perfect Continuous.

options.text: He said that he has been waiting for me since morning.
options.explanation: The tense shift is incorrect; it should be Past Perfect Continuous.

options.text: He said that he had been waiting for me since morning.
options.explanation: The tense shift is correct; Present Perfect Continuous changes to Past Perfect Continuous.

options.text: He said that he would be waiting for me since morning.
options.explanation: The tense shift is incorrect; it should be Past Perfect Continuous.

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the past tense ('said'), the Present Perfect Continuous tense in Direct Speech ('have been waiting') changes to the Past Perfect Continuous tense ('had been waiting') in Indirect Speech.
questions.hint: The reporting verb is in the past tense, so the tense in the reported speech must shift back.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Consider the sentence: 'If I ______ a bird, I ______ fly.' Which pair of verbs correctly completes this sentence to express an unreal condition in the present?

questions.question: Look! The children _________ in the park right now.

options.explanation: The simple past tense is incorrect for actions happening now.
The simple present tense is incorrect for actions happening now.
The present continuous tense is used for actions happening at the moment of speaking.
The verb should agree with the plural subject 'children'.

questions.explanation: The action is happening at the moment of speaking, indicated by 'Look!' and 'right now,' requiring the present continuous tense. 'Children' is a plural subject, so 'are playing' is the correct verb form.
questions.hint: The present continuous tense is used for actions happening at the moment of speaking.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: I think it _________ tomorrow.

options.explanation: The simple past tense is incorrect for future events.
The simple present tense is incorrect for future events.
The simple future tense is used for predictions about future events.
The present perfect tense is incorrect for future events.

questions.explanation: The word 'tomorrow' indicates a future event, and 'I think' suggests a prediction, making the simple future tense ('will rain') appropriate.
questions.hint: Future events use the simple future tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is in the Present Perfect Tense?

options.explanation: This sentence is in the present continuous tense.
This sentence uses 'have' + past participle, forming the present perfect tense.
This sentence is in the simple past tense.

options.text: We will go for a picnic.
options.explanation: This sentence is in the simple future tense.

questions.explanation: The present perfect tense is formed with 'has/have' + the past participle of the main verb. Option B, 'They have finished their work,' correctly follows this structure.
questions.hint: The present perfect tense uses 'has/have' + past participle.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct indirect speech for: He said, 'I am watching a movie.'

options.text: He said that he was watching a movie.
options.explanation: The present continuous tense changes to past continuous, and the pronoun 'I' changes to 'he'.

options.text: He said that I was watching a movie.
options.explanation: The pronoun 'I' should change to 'he' to reflect the speaker.

options.text: He said that he is watching a movie.
options.explanation: The tense should shift back to past continuous in indirect speech.

options.text: He said that he had watched a movie.
options.explanation: The tense should be past continuous, not past perfect.

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the past tense ('said'), the present continuous tense in direct speech ('am watching') changes to the past continuous tense ('was watching') in indirect speech. The pronoun 'I' also changes to 'he' to reflect the speaker.
questions.hint: In indirect speech, the tense shifts back one step when the reporting verb is in the past tense.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Choose the correct passive voice for: My mother baked a cake yesterday.

options.text: A cake was baked by my mother yesterday.
options.explanation: The object 'a cake' becomes the subject, and the verb changes to 'was baked'.

options.text: A cake is baked by my mother yesterday.
options.explanation: The simple present tense is incorrect for a past action.

options.text: A cake had been baked by my mother yesterday.
options.explanation: The past perfect tense is incorrect for a simple past action.

options.text: My mother was baked a cake yesterday.
options.explanation: The subject and object are incorrectly swapped.

questions.explanation: The original sentence is in the simple past tense ('baked'). In the passive voice, the simple past becomes 'was/were' + the past participle of the main verb. Since 'A cake' is singular, 'was baked' is the correct form.
questions.hint: In passive voice, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject, and the verb changes to 'was/were' + past participle.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: If you study hard, you _________ good marks.

options.explanation: The modal 'would' is incorrect for Type 1 conditionals.
The simple future tense is used in the main clause of Type 1 conditionals.
The simple present tense is incorrect for the main clause in Type 1 conditionals.
The simple past tense is incorrect for the main clause in Type 1 conditionals.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 1 conditional sentence, which expresses a real and possible condition and its likely result. The 'if' clause uses the simple present tense ('study'), and the main clause uses the simple future tense ('will get').
questions.hint: Type 1 conditionals use the simple present tense in the 'if' clause and the simple future tense in the main clause.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: I _________ to Agra last year, but I _________ the Taj Mahal yet.

options.explanation: The simple past tense is used for the completed past action, and the present perfect tense is used for the action that has not happened yet.
The present perfect tense is incorrect for a completed past action.
The simple present and future tense are incorrect for the given context.
The past perfect tense is incorrect for a simple past action.

questions.explanation: 'Last year' clearly indicates a completed action in a specific past time, requiring the simple past tense ('went'). 'Yet' indicates an action that has not happened up to the present moment, requiring the present perfect tense ('haven't seen').
questions.hint: Use the simple past tense for completed past actions and the present perfect tense for actions that have not happened up to now.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: If he _________ the instructions carefully, he _________ the experiment correctly.

options.explanation: The past perfect tense is used in the 'if' clause, and 'would have' + past participle is used in the main clause for Type 3 conditionals.
The simple past tense is incorrect for the 'if' clause in Type 3 conditionals.
The simple present and future tense are incorrect for Type 3 conditionals.
The main clause should use 'would have' + past participle for Type 3 conditionals.

questions.explanation: This is a Type 3 conditional sentence, used to express an unreal or impossible condition in the past and its hypothetical past result. The 'if' clause uses the past perfect tense ('had followed'), and the main clause uses 'would have' + the past participle ('would have performed').
questions.hint: Type 3 conditionals use the past perfect tense in the 'if' clause and 'would have' + past participle in the main clause.
questions.subject: upbo11-english

questions.question: Assertion (A): The sentence 'By next month, I will have completed my project' correctly uses the Future Perfect Tense. Reason (R): The Future Perfect Tense is used to describe an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: The reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: The assertion is true.

questions.explanation: The assertion correctly identifies the tense as Future Perfect Tense (formed with 'will have' + past participle) and its appropriate usage with the time marker 'By next month.' The reason accurately defines the function of the Future Perfect Tense, which is to express an action that will be finished before a specified point in the future. Thus, R correctly explains A.
questions.hint: The Future Perfect Tense is used for actions that will be completed before a specific future time.
